questions.prompt: Holes in n-type silicon have \(D_p = 12\ \mathrm{cm^2/s}\) and \(\tau_p = 0.5\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). What is the diffusion length \(L_p = \sqrt{D_p\tau_p}\), in µm?
questions.explanation:
\[L_p = \sqrt{12\times0.5\times10^{-6}} = \sqrt{6\times10^{-6}}\ \mathrm{cm} = 2.45\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{cm} \approx 24.5\ \mu\mathrm{m}\]
Common mistake: forgetting the square root, or entering \(\tau\) in µs (giving 2.45 cm).

questions.prompt: Excess holes are continuously injected at \(x = 0\) into a long n-type region, with \(\Delta p(\infty) = 0\). In steady state, \(\frac{d^2\Delta p}{dx^2} = \frac{\Delta p}{L_p^2}\). What is the profile?
options: \(\Delta p(x) = \Delta p(0)(1 - x/L_p)\)
\(\Delta p(x) = \Delta p(0)\,e^{-x/L_p}\)
\(\Delta p(x) = \Delta p(0)\,e^{+x/L_p}\)
\(\Delta p(x) = \Delta p(0)\cos(x/L_p)\)
questions.explanation:
The general solution is \(Ae^{-x/L_p} + Be^{x/L_p}\) (reader Eq. 6.13). \(\Delta p(\infty) = 0\) forces \(B = 0\), and the value at \(x = 0\) gives \(A = \Delta p(0)\).
A straight line is the no-recombination (short-region) case. A cosine would solve \(\Delta p'' = -\Delta p/L^2\), which has the wrong sign.
questions.figure_alt: Excess hole concentration Δp(x) decaying exponentially from Δp(0) at x = 0; at x = Lp it has fallen to Δp(0)/e.

questions.prompt: What does the diffusion length \(L_p\) represent physically?
options: The typical distance an excess minority carrier diffuses before it recombines; at x = Lp the excess has fallen to 1/e of its starting value
The width of the depletion region
The distance a carrier moves between collisions
The distance at which the excess has fallen exactly to zero
questions.explanation:
\(L_p = \sqrt{D_p\tau_p}\) combines how fast carriers spread (\(D_p\)) with how long they last (\(\tau_p\)). It's typically micrometres to millimetres, far longer than the mean free path (about 10 nm) and usually longer than the depletion width.
An exponential never reaches exactly zero; after \(3L_p\) about 5% remains.

questions.prompt: Excess holes are injected with \(\Delta p(0) = 10^{14}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) into a long n-region with \(L_p = 25\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). What is \(\Delta p\) at \(x = 50\ \mu\mathrm{m}\)? Scientific notation is fine.
questions.explanation:
\[\Delta p(50\ \mu m) = 10^{14}e^{-50/25} = 10^{14}e^{-2} \approx 1.35\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\]
Two diffusion lengths, so \(e^{-2} \approx 13.5\%\) is left.
questions.figure_alt: Exponential decay of injected excess holes with distance.

questions.prompt: Holes are injected into a long n-region with \(\Delta p(0) = 10^{14}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), \(D_p = 12\ \mathrm{cm^2/s}\) and \(L_p = 24.5\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). What is the hole diffusion current density at \(x = 0\), in mA/cm²?
questions.explanation:
\[J_p(x) = -qD_p\frac{d\Delta p}{dx} = \frac{qD_p\Delta p(0)}{L_p}e^{-x/L_p}\]
\[J_p(0) = \frac{(1.602\times10^{-19})(12)(10^{14})}{2.45\times10^{-3}} = 7.85\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{A/cm^2} \approx 78.5\ \mathrm{mA/cm^2}\]
It's like a linear profile that drops to zero over one diffusion length. (Reader Eq. 6.15 leaves out the factor \(qD_p\) in this result. That's a typo; the units only work with it.)
questions.figure_alt: Exponential excess hole profile; the slope at x = 0 sets the diffusion current.

questions.prompt: Same region (\(J_p(0) = 78.5\ \mathrm{mA/cm^2}\)). What is the hole diffusion current density at \(x = L_p\), in mA/cm²?
questions.explanation:
The current is proportional to the slope, which decays like the profile itself:
\[J_p(L_p) = J_p(0)e^{-1} = 78.5\times0.368 \approx 28.9\ \mathrm{mA/cm^2}\]
The 'missing' hole current became recombination between 0 and \(L_p\). The next question asks where it went.

questions.prompt: In the long n-region above, the hole current decays as \(e^{-x/L_p}\), yet in steady state the TOTAL current through the device has to be the same at every \(x\). How?
options: The total current also decays; charge builds up in the n-region
The lost holes leave through the sides of the device
Displacement current makes up the difference
Majority electrons carry the rest: an electron current flows in to recombine with the holes, so Jₙ(x) + Jₚ(x) = Jₚ(0) everywhere
questions.explanation:
Each recombination removes one hole and one electron. The electrons come from the n-contact as majority current, so where \(J_p\) shrinks, \(J_n\) grows by the same amount (reader Sec. 6.4.3).
Gotcha: 'current decays' sounds like charge is lost, but it only changes CARRIER TYPE. In steady state nothing builds up and nothing changes in time, so there's no displacement current.
questions.figure_alt: Hole current density Jp(x) decaying exponentially from Jp(0); the remainder of the constant total current is carried by electrons.

questions.prompt: In that long n-region, what fraction of the total current is carried by HOLES at \(x = 2L_p\)?
questions.explanation:
The total current equals \(J_p(0)\) everywhere, and the hole part is \(J_p(0)e^{-x/L_p}\):
\[\frac{J_p(2L_p)}{J_{total}} = e^{-2} \approx 0.135\]
The other 86.5% is electron current at that point. By about 5 diffusion lengths, essentially all the current is carried by majority carriers, as in an ordinary resistor.

questions.prompt: An n-region is only \(W = 1\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) long, with \(L_p = 25\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). Holes are injected at \(x = 0\), and an ohmic contact at \(x = W\) holds \(\Delta p(W) = 0\). What does the excess-hole profile look like?
options: An exponential with decay length Lp, cut off at W
An exponential with decay length W
Nearly a straight line from Δp(0) to 0: almost no recombination happens, so the hole current is nearly the same at every x
Flat at Δp(0) up to W, then a sudden drop to zero
questions.explanation:
With \(W \ll L_p\), the \(\Delta p/L_p^2\) term is negligible: \(\Delta p'' \approx 0\), so the profile is LINEAR (reader Sec. 6.5.2 and Fig. 6.11). A constant slope means a constant current: \(J_p = qD_p\Delta p(0)/W\).
Gotcha: copying the long-region exponential gets both the shape and the current wrong. The current is larger by about \(L_p/W\), because the gradient is much steeper.

questions.prompt: Preview of the diode equation: holes are injected with \(\Delta p(0) = 10^{14}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) into a SHORT n-region of width \(W_n = 2\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) (\(\ll L_p\)), with \(D_p = 12\ \mathrm{cm^2/s}\). What hole current density flows, in A/cm²?
questions.explanation:
Linear profile, so the slope is \(\Delta p(0)/W_n\):
\[J_p = \frac{qD_p\Delta p(0)}{W_n} = \frac{(1.602\times10^{-19})(12)(10^{14})}{2\times10^{-4}} \approx 0.961\ \mathrm{A/cm^2}\]
That's about 12.2 times the long-region value, because \(L_p/W_n\) is that big. In the diode skill, \(\Delta p(0)\) is set by the applied voltage.

questions.prompt: Preview of the bipolar transistor: a BJT injects minority electrons into a thin p-type 'base', and they must diffuse across it to be collected on the other side. Why is the base made much thinner than the electrons' diffusion length \(L_n\)?
options: So that the electrons recombine quickly, which keeps the transistor cool
So that almost every injected electron crosses before it recombines; recombination in the base would waste current
To make the electron profile exponential instead of linear
Because a thin base has a longer lifetime
questions.explanation:
With \(W_B \ll L_n\) the profile is nearly linear, and only a tiny fraction (of order \((W_B/L_n)^2\)) of the electrons recombine. So the current that leaves is almost all of the current injected.
That near-perfect transfer is what makes 'transistor action' possible; the BJT skills build on it.

questions.prompt: Preview of forward-biased diodes: forward bias \(V\) raises the hole concentration at the edge of an n-region to \(p_{n0}e^{V/(kT/q)}\), so \(\Delta p(0) = p_{n0}(e^{V/V_{th}} - 1)\). For \(N_D = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) (\(p_{n0} = 10^{4}\)) and \(V = 0.6\ \mathrm{V}\) (\(V_{th} = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\)), with a long n-region (\(D_p = 12\ \mathrm{cm^2/s}\), \(L_p = 24.5\ \mu\mathrm{m}\)), find the hole current density at the edge, in mA/cm².
questions.explanation:
\[\Delta p(0) = 10^{4}\left(e^{0.6/0.026} - 1\right) = 10^{4}e^{23.08} \approx 1.05\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\]
\[J_p = \frac{qD_p\Delta p(0)}{L_p} = \frac{(1.602\times10^{-19})(12)(1.05\times10^{14})}{2.45\times10^{-3}} \approx 82.6\ \mathrm{mA/cm^2}\]
Every 60 mV of extra forward bias multiplies this by 10: the exponential diode law.
